claims.text: Retention of atomic-scale strain fields is the key factor governing the structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles at the stated service temperatures.
Rapid quenching induces or retains atomic-scale strain fields in the nanoparticles.
Retained strain fields create kinetic barriers to elemental diffusion.
Retained strain fields suppress elemental segregation and phase decomposition.
Preservation of a homogeneous chemical state is required for stable catalytic activity.
Retained strain fields maintain thermoelectric performance during high-temperature operation.
The selected initial nanoparticles have homogeneous elemental distributions.
The selected initial nanoparticles possess inherent lattice-strain heterogeneity.
Rapid post-synthesis quenching locks in and maximizes atomic-scale strain fields relative to slow cooling.
Conventional slow cooling partially relaxes atomic-scale strain fields.
Retained lattice strain increases local configurational entropy.
Retained lattice strain reduces atomic mobility.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit less elemental segregation during service than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit less phase decomposition during service than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain catalytic and thermoelectric performance better than slow-cooled nanoparticles.
The proposed strain-mediated effect is significant only in near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles with sufficient initial strain heterogeneity.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to inherently ordered nanoparticles.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to nanoparticles that are already compositionally segregated after synthesis.
The proposed effect may not occur if quenching and slow cooling do not produce measurably different strain states.
Reactive atmospheres may alter surface chemistry independently of bulk strain.
